content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies membership inference attacks for text-to-image generation models, including diffusion-based models and sequence-to-sequence models. This paper proposes four attack methodologies for membership information attacks. The experiments show the proposed attacks achieve good performance. The paper also empirically studies factors that affect attack performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This paper introduces new attack methodologies to a new domain, which contributes value to the community. The experiment results show promising results for the proposed attack methods. 
2. The proposed approach is well-motivated. Four attack methods are motivated by three reasonable intuitions. 
3. This paper provides extensive experiments to study the attack methods. It considers two different models, diffusion-based and sequence-to-sequence models. It also provides an ablation study to analyze the effect of different factors on attack performance.
4. This paper is well-written and easy to follow.

Weakness:
1. This paper can improve on discussing the difference between the proposed attack methods and existing attack methods for image generation models. Do the four attack methods also work for general image generation models when we remove the imaging captioning part? If so, how do they compare with existing attack methods in general image generation models? 
2. It will be good to have more discussion comparing the assumptions in this paper with existing work. It is unclear to me if the auxiliary dataset is a strong assumption.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is easy to follow and has good quality. The problem studied in this paper is new. It will be good to have more discussions to compare with previous work to clarify the novelty. The experiments could be reproducible with the details provided in this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper studied an interesting problem and contribute new values to the community. The paper is well written. It can be improved by clarifying the novelty. I recommend 6: marginally above the acceptance threshold
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for membership inference attacks against text-to-image models. The authors utilize the vision-language model to generate a caption of the query image, feed it into the victim model, and then distinguish the membership based on the quality, reconstruction error, and textual semantics of the generated image. Experimental results show the high membership inference accuracy of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This is the first work that applies membership inference attacks to text-to-image models. It empirically shows the privacy issues of the state-of-the-art text-to-image models.
- The method only requires a single query to the victim model, which reduces the possibility of being detected and lowers the computational cost.

Concerns:
- In sections 4.1 and 4.2, the meaning of "quality" in Intuition I and Attack I is unclear. The attack directly feeds the generated image or its embedding into the attack model, which is not necessarily related to the quality of the generated image.
- In section 5.1, the architectures of Attack I-P/II-P and Attack-IV should be clarified (e.g., the number of the CNN layers, and the embedding size of the sub-network).
- The experimental results show that same-modality embedding works better than cross-modality embedding. What is the intuition behind it?
- In the experiments, the members and non-members are from different datasets (The former are from LAION for LDM and CC3M for CALL-E, while the latter are from MSCOCO and Visual Genome). It seems that the difference between members and non-members is more a transferability issue than a membership inference issue.
- The core novelty of this work is the use of the vision-language model to generate the input of victim models. However, previous studies (e.g., GAN-Leaks) have shown that finding latent features with the minimal difference between the query image and generated image and measuring such difference can successfully inference the membership of the generation model. This work empirically shows how image captioning can be used in the process of finding inputs.
  - GAN-Leaks: A Taxonomy of Membership Inference Attacks against Generative Models
    <https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03935>

Minor comments:
- Section 4.2: In the description of Attack I, "... feeding the query image directly into the attack model" should be "... feeding the generated image directly into the attack model".
- Section 4.2: In the description of Attack II, "The former, Attack II-S, ..." should be "The former, Attack II-P, ..."
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This work is novel because it is the first to apply membership inference attacks to text-to-image models.
Clarity can be improved. 
Experiments are not convincing enough, which decreases the overall quality.
content.summary_of_the_review: The first work that applies membership inference attacks to text-to-image models, but the experiments are not convincing enough.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a set of membership inference attacks on text-to-image diffusion models. These attacks are based on three key intuitions that authors describe. The proposed attacks are evaluated on two models: Latent Diffusion representing diffusion-based models, and DALL-E 2 mini representing sequence-to-sequence models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
* The paper presents the first study on membership inference attack on text-to-image generative models.

**Weaknesses**
* Insufficient motivation / theory
  * Sec 4.1 lists three intuitions the proposed attacks are based on, but there is no justification for why these particular intuitions are important, other than that ML models have "overfitting nature."  While they are sensible, it would be nice if the authors could further justify them in a more principled manner.
  * Please correct me if I'm missing something, but it's unclear whether the proposed evaluation method properly captures the attack model's ability to perform membership inference.  If the attacker has a single query image $x$, how can the proposed method perform membership inference on $x$?  My understanding is that the proposed method is not applicable in this case, unless we make the assumption that $x$ came from a dataset that we can use as the member dataset.
  * The authors list the fact that only one model call is required for each query image as an advantage of the proposed method. However, given that the attacker need to first construct a dataset to train the attack model on, the total number of model calls is still relatively large (e.g. 30k in the presented experiments).  It would be nice to see a more detailed justification for this, with a concrete scenario under which the proposed method is advantageous in terms of sample complexity.
     * Note that even the smallest portion in Figures 6 & 9 use 5% of the member dataset, which is still too large (1500 samples) for a realistic membership inference scenario.

* Empirical results are lacking in rigor and clarity.
  * Need for baseline: In Sec 5.2, authors claim that the achieved accuracy (e.g. even the lowest one was 0.65) is "remarkable."  However in the absence of a reasonable baseline method, it's unclear how to interpret this performance aside from a rather uninformative fact that it's better than random guess.  Based on the way auxiliary datasets are created (e.g. using completely different datasets for members vs. non-members), I'm rather skeptical of this performance metric. 
  * Sec 5.2 states "We reason that this is due to the fact that these pixel-level features make pixels independent and are unable to obtain context-dependent information, whereas semantic-level features have this capability."  I don't understand what this means.  In what sense does using pixel-level features "make pixels independent"?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**
As mentioned in above comments, the paper uses rather vague language and lacks sufficient justification for their design choices.

**Quality**
Writing quality is questionable, as evidenced by somewhat confusing experimental results and lack of baseline comparisons.

**Novelty**
Novelty is lacking, as the proposed evaluation is a straightforward implementation of the three intuitions, and the intuitions themselves are not very novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while I believe the task of membership inference on text-to-image generative models is important, the paper lacks sufficient justifications and experimental rigor to support for acceptance.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops a variety of membership inference attacks, to try to determine if a given image or image-caption pair was used to train a text-to-image generative model. All considered attacks achieve nontrivial accuracy, with attacks based on semantic embeddings achieving high accuracies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper proposes and evaluates a variety of sensible attacks on two different, modern generative models.

Weaknesses:
- The true efficacy of the attacks is unclear due to insufficient empirical evaluation (see below).
- The attacks are not particularly novel.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I'm very concerned by the evaluation being entirely based on comparing datasets known to be in the training set to "local" datasets which are, well, different datasets. I haven't run the experiment, and it seems that you haven't easier, but based on results from two-sample testing – see e.g. [Lopez-Paz and Oquab (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06545) and [Liu et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.09116) – I _strongly_ expect that a classifier can easily distinguish between, say, Laion-Face and MSCOCO-Face. Indeed, your FID score result shows that the mean and/or covariance of Inception embedding features is quite different between the two datasets. This seems to be exactly what Attack I does, either based on raw image pixels or based on CLIP embeddings, if I'm correctly understanding your sentence "For simplicity, an adversary can differentiate between members or non-members by feeding the query image directly into the attack model, rather than measuring quality and then making the distinction." That this method (particularly the -S variant) essentially works seems to be an enormous red flag, since if I'm understanding correctly your method for testing whether a generative model has seen an image _doesn't even look at the model_. (Nor does it look at the text, if I'm understanding right.)

The best models in your study are based on Attack II-S and Attack 4, which includes the data used by II-S as input and never seems to perform any differently than II-S, so let's assume that Attack 4 is essentially identical to Attack II-S. This attack does at least use the generative model, unlike Attack I, so that's good. But it still is testing whether the image->caption->image process works well on two different datasets with different characteristics, which might be due entirely to different characteristics of the datasets rather than the model actually overfitting to the particular query images.

One way to test this would be to retrain LDM or DALL-E mini with a small percentage of the dataset randomly held out, and use those as non-members (with a train-test split for your attack as well). I can't immediately tell if either model kept a held-out validation or test set, so, you might have to retrain. For DALL-E mini this is not really feasible; I don't immediately see how expensive LDM was to train on LAION-400m, but the pretrained models at least probably use a validation split on ImageNet. This is annoying, but I really don't see any other way to at all tell whether your work is checking what it claims to be checking.

Without a thorough analysis of this issue, I do not see any way that this paper can support its claims.
content.summary_of_the_review: I'm not at all convinced that the attack accuracy here is a reasonable metric, and so there's no way to tell whether the empirical evaluation here is meaningful without doing that kind of analysis.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
